Consider the vector $\mathbf{v}$ and the rotation-scaling matrix $C$ shown above. Given that $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of a $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=-1-4\textrm{i},$ find a matrix $P$ such that $A=PCP^{-1}.$
examples.worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2 \times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PCP^{-1},$ where 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071601/assets/9fb15e52a1df912c9e5fb4238f45d705cd0a56fb7190620c0f0fd597f9a2b8c0.png)

and $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda.$

First, notice that 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071601/assets/80bd36915851e6ebeb67befe8af41e5496fa5491b9d87c294d8b937eb586319f.png)

Next, we can find the real and imaginary parts of our eigenvector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1+2\text{i}\end{aligned}]={{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Re}(v)}+\text{i}{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Im}(v)}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can now construct $P\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}-7 & -2 \\ 2 & -7\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $P$ and the rotation-scaling matrix $C$ shown above. Given that $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ what are the eigenvalues and the corresponding eigenvectors of $A?$
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2\times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}],
$$

and $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda .$

- From the matrix $C=[\begin{aligned}-7 & -2 \\ -(-2) & -7\end{aligned}],$ we deduce that $\text{Re}(\lambda )=-7$ and $\text{Im}(\lambda )=-2.$ So, our eigenvalue is

$$
\lambda =-7+(-2)\text{i}=-7-2\text{i}.
$$

- From the matrix $P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}],$ we deduce that our corresponding eigenvector is

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1+(-2)\text{i} \\ -3+2\text{i}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1-2\text{i} \\ -3+2\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, the second eigenvalue of $A$ must be the complex conjugate of $\lambda ,$ and the second eigenvector must be the complex conjugate of $v.$

Therefore, our eigenvalues and eigenvectors are 

$$
\lambda =-7∓2\text{i},\,v=[\begin{aligned}1∓2\text{i} \\ -3\pm 2\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$
